missingNumbers.existingAnchor: A one point rise in the projected federal deficit over GDP raises long-term interest rates about 25 basis points, and the rates states pay to borrow move with them. A law that cuts spending lowers what every state pays; a law that spends more raises it. Markets price the projected deficit when the law is made, so there is no lag. The paper's summary gives no band, so the spread is the default for researched links, 25% either way.
missingNumbers.existingSource: Laubach 2009, New Evidence on the Interest Rate Effects of Budget Deficits and Debt, Journal of the European Economic Association 7(4): 858-885; the deficit change from data/research/federal/federal-outlay-terms-fy2025.json (Treasury Monthly Treasury Statement, BEA, CBO)

missingNumbers.existingAnchor: A state that gets a dollar more of military procurement than others gets about $1.50 more output. Earnings are read to move one for one with output, so each percent of the state's output that extra contracts add lifts earnings 1.5%. The extra contracts follow a build-up at the pace defense contracts rose in the years they beat inflation, in each state in proportion to the contracts it drew in 2024 (data/research/federal/defense-contracts-by-state-fy2024.json). The paper's summary gives no band, so the spread is the default for researched links, 25% either way. The effect is read the same year the money is spent, since the study measures it within the year and the build-up already phases in over the years of the law.
missingNumbers.existingSource: Nakamura and Steinsson 2014, Fiscal Stimulus in a Monetary Union: Evidence from U.S. Regions, American Economic Review 104(3), NBER w17391; contracts from USAspending.gov and output from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, read September 29, 2026
